A 28-year-old man with congenital aortic stenosis underwent a Ross procedure during childhood. Ten years later he developed severe aortic regurgitation of the pulmonary autograft and required reoperative aortic root replacement (AVR) with a mechanical valve conduit. One year ago, pulmonary stenosis of his homograft was treated with a transcatheter valve replacement. He presents now with a 4-week history of fevers and chills, and 2 blood cultures that are positive for Streptococcus bovis. options: 6-week course of aqueous crystalline penicillin G plus gentamicin
Mediastinal exploration and omental flap coverage

Re-repair the valve with a posterior leaflet sliding plasty

stem: A 43-year-old, otherwise healthy man with symptomatic mitral regurgitation has been referred for mitral valve repair. A transesophageal echo demonstrates a Barlow's valve with diffuse anterior and posterior leaflet prolapse. The best management is
options: Neochords to posterior and anterior leaflets and annuloplasty ring

stem: A 65-year-old man underwent mitral valve repair with triangular resection and 32 mm semi-rigid complete annuloplasty ring. On separation from cardiopulmonary bypass, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior leaflet is seen. The best next step is to:
options: Remove the annuloplasty ring and replace it with a 28 mm ring
Perform a sliding plasty of the posterior leaflet
Place a stitch between leaflet scallops A3 and P3
Replace the mitral valve, preserving the anterior leaflet

Ascending aortic graft replacement and AVR

MV replacement with a mechanical valve
Placement of an intra-aortic balloon pump

stem: A 54-year-old man underwent mitral valve (MV) repair for mitral regurgitation (MR). Post-procedure echocardiography showed trivial MR. He was discharged to home with a hematocrit of 36%. stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with increasing dyspnea on exertion. She had been followed for mitral valve (MV) prolapse and moderate mitral regurgitation (MR). Her urine pregnancy test is now positive, and a sonogram reveals a fetus of 13-14 weeks gestational age. She relates that she has been unable to lie flat for the past couple of nights. She is adamant that she desires the pregnancy. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, and resting respiratory rate is 24/min. She has gained 30 pounds in the past month. Her peripheral pulses are 2-3+ and 3+ pedal edema is evident bilaterally. Echocardiography reveals severe central MR with pulmonary vein flow reversal, an enlarged left atrium, and moderate bileaflet prolapse. The best management is to
options: Treat with medical therapy throughout the pregnancy
Maintain medical therapy now, but advise MV surgery at 30 weeks gestational age
Perform a transcatheter MV repair now

stem: A 35-year-old woman underwent mitral valve commissurotomy and ring annuloplasty for rheumatic valvular disease. Fifteen months later, she presented with vague neurologic symptoms and an embolic stroke involving a posterior cerebellar artery was documented. Blood cultures are now positive for Candida tropicalis and an echocardiogram shows moderate mitral stenosis and a 0.5 x 0.4 cm vegetation on the annuloplasty ring. In addition to treatment with amphotericin B, the best management is to
options: Complete a full course of Amphotericin B and repeat blood cultures
Switch to and complete course of newer antifungal agents (e.g., flucytosine) and repeat blood cultures
List the patient for a heart transplant

options: Surgical aortic valve replacement (AVR) via hemisternotomy

Cardiac catheterization demonstrated normal coronary arteries. An image from the preoperative chest CT scan is shown. Following mitral valve replacement, a glistening hematoma near the left atrial appendage is noted. An intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram shows a well-seated prosthesis. The best next step is
options: Administer protamine and avoid manipulating the heart
Administer protamine and pack the hematoma with gel foam and thrombin
Resume cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and place a bovine pericardial patch over the hematoma

stem: A 35-year-old woman had an idiopathic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction 35%. There was 4+ mitral regurgitation from posterior leaflet prolapse, pulmonary hypertension (70/30 mmHg), and 4+ tricuspid regurgitation. At surgery, exposure of the mitral valve was difficult due to biventricular enlargement. The echo clip is from the intraoperative transesophageal study following mitral valve repair and tricuspid valve repair (see CD). The best next step is

Volume administration and vasopressor support with neosynephrine
Resumption of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and re-replacement of the mitral valve prosthesis
Resumption of CPB and replacement of the aortic valve

stem: A 60-year-old man was admitted with a stroke, unable to move his left arm or left leg. An image from a CT scan and clips from a transesophageal echo are shown (see CD). Intravenous antibiotics were started. The patient is ventilator dependent due to severe congestive heart failure and requires moderate inotropic support with epinephrine. A surgical evaluation was requested. The best next step is

6 weeks of antibiotic therapy before proceeding with MVR
Referral for transcatheter mitral valve procedure

The chest CT reveals a moderate left pulmonary contusion and hemothorax, while the right side has a minor pulmonary contusion with no hemothorax. There are no bony injuries on either side. The best next step is
options: Bilateral chest tubes and epidural pain catheter
Left chest tube and aggressive pulmonary toilet
Bilateral chest tubes and VATS if output > 250 mL/hr x 2 hours
Immediate VATS exploration of the left chest

stem: A 26-year-old man sustained a gunshot wound to the right chest. The entry site is in the midclavicular line just below the nipple. Initial vital signs were a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, a systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L nasal cannula. He was alert and complained of chest pain and shortness of breath. A FAST examination showed no pericardial fluid, but the CXR revealed a complete white out of the right hemithorax and a normal cardiac silhouette. A right chest tube was placed and yielded 1000 mL of blood. A repeat CXR showed improved aeration, but there was a residual hemothorax. Over the next 3 hours he had bloody chest tube outputs of 250, 250, and 400 mL. He has become increasingly tachycardic. He requires fluid boluses to support his blood pressure and a non-rebreather to maintain oxygenation. The best next step is
options: IV fluid boluses and increased chest tube suction
Starting pressors and placement of another
Right VATS exploration right exploratory thoracotomy

stem: A 50-year-old woman underwent a right upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection 3 days ago for a T3N2M0 lung cancer. On postoperative day 4, she developed increased milky output from her chest tube with a triglyceride level of 150 mg/dL, with a total chest tube output of 2500 mL. Her regular diet was changed to a low fat diet with medium chain triglycerides and chest tube outputs remained > 1 L/day for the following 48 hours. The best management is
options: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) and bedside pleurodesis
Exploration and placement of clips in the mediastinum

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a 5-year history of myasthenia gravis underwent imaging recently due to increasing symptoms. An anterior mediastinal mass was identified. Her myasthenic symptoms consist of moderate bulbar muscle weakness and occasional mild limb weakness. She is currently on pyridostigmine 120 mg three times a day and has had multiple courses of steroids in the past. After consultation with her neurologist, her medical therapy was optimized and a robotic thymectomy was performed. In the operating room the patient is unable to achieve an adequate tidal volume for extubation after surgery. The best next step is to
options: Extubate in the operating room and place on noninvasive ventilation
Wait 10 minutes and repeat the reversal agents
Transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU) and consider high-dose steroid therapy and/or plasmapheresis
Transfer to the ICU, rest overnight on the ventilator, and plan a sniff test to evaluate her phrenic nerve function

stem: An 18-year-old man was involved in a high speed motor vehicle crash. He has visible right-sided chest wall bruising, a Glasgow Coma Scale reading of 13, and stable vital signs: heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 115/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. Imaging reveals a small subdural hematoma and 3 nondisplaced rib fractures with a pulmonary contusion. The next morning, the CXR shows increasing right lower lobe opacification and he requires a non-rebreather mask. A right side chest tube is placed. There is minimal output and a small air leak. His hemoglobin is 12 gm/dL, down from 15 gm/dL on admission; his pain score is 8, and he has a good cough. The best next step is
options: Stat chest CT to assess for bleeding and to plan operative intervention for rib fixation
Place an additional chest tube on the right and continue pain control measures
Continue supportive respiratory care with intubation as needed and pain control for the rib fractures
Plan for operative rib fixation and possible lower lobectomy

stem: A 23-year-old man was brought into the emergency department (ED) after a motor vehicle crash. He was a restrained front seat passenger involved in a head on collision and was intubated at the scene. On arrival in the ED, a CXR revealed a complete right side pneumothorax. A right chest tube was placed and a large blowing air leak was evident. Due to progressive subcutaneous emphysema, a second chest tube was placed, but a CXR showed incomplete resolution of the pneumothorax. It is currently difficult to maintain tidal volumes on the ventilator. The best next management is
options: Plan for rigid bronchoscopy and airway stenting
Plan for bronchoscopy and right thoracotomy
Increase suction on both chest tubes
Transfer to the intensive care unit for bronchoscopy

stem: A 66-year-old diabetic man underwent resection of a stage IIA non-small cell lung cancer, squamous cell histology. Adjuvant therapy with cisplatin plus vinorelbine was initiated 6 weeks later. After 2 cycles of treatment he was admitted to the ICU with respiratory failure and acute renal failure (creatinine 2.7 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.8 mg/dL). The most likely cause for the new renal insufficiency is
options: Renal injury related to tumor lysis syndrome

stem: An 86-year-old woman had a VATS right upper lobectomy for non-small cell lung cancer 2 days ago. Her oxygen requirements have acutely increased from 2 to 6 L via nasal cannula, and her CXR shows worsening air space disease in the mid right lung field. Her WBC count is 16,500 lipl- and there is progressive metabolic acidosis. Bedside flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy shows minimal secretions, but the right middle lobe orifice cannot be traversed. The best next step is
options: Stenting of the right middle lobe bronchus
Antibiotic therapy for hospital acquired pneumonia
Steroids and diuresis to reduce right middle lobe mucosal edema

stem: A patient is now 2 years status post right pneumonectomy for stage IIB non-small cell lung cancer. He reports worsening dyspnea even at rest over the past 6 months. He presents to the emergency department with severe shortness of breath where a chest CT was negative for pulmonary embolism. He has been admitted to the ICU. The best next step is
options: Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter

stem: A 54-year-old man is 3 years status post single lung transplantation for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Over the past 6 months he has developed progressive dyspnea on exertion and exercise intolerance. His FEV1 has decreased by approximately 15%. The most recent chest CT scan shows slow hyperinflation of his native lung. Recent bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy rule out chronic rejection and anastomotic stricture. The best next step is
options: Consideration for lung volume reduction surgery
Dynamic CT scan with airway reconstructions

stem: A 55-year-old woman underwent an Ivor Lewis esophagectomy for an esophageal adenocarcinoma after neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy. Her postoperative course was uncomplicated and she was advanced to a regular diet and discharged to home on postoperative day 7. One week after discharge she now complains of dizziness, abdominal pain, and severe diarrhea 30 minutes after eating. She states, "The food runs right through me, especially when I eat ice cream. I feel tired and have to lie down after eating". Her vital signs are stable and the physical examination is unremarkable. A complete blood count and serum chemistry shows a low serum potassium level (3.8 mEq/L), but laboratory results are otherwise within normal limits. She is concerned that something is wrong with the "new bowel connection." The best next step is to
options: Reassure her that her symptoms are not unusual and will resolve over time
Increase the fiber content in her diet and avoid high sugar containing foods
Start her on subcutaneous octreotide at 50 µg 5 min before each meal
Replace her potassium loss with 20 mEq of potassium daily by mouth

stem: A woman underwent a transthoracic esophagectomy with cervical anastomosis for a mid-esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Postoperatively, the patient is hoarse and has difficulty clearing her sputum. On postoperative day 5, she is unable to complete the planned contrast esophagogram. She coughs violently while ingesting the contrast and there is radiologic evidence of significant glottic penetration. The best next step is
options: Replacement of a nasogastric tube until her voice and swallowing improve
Laryngoscopy and vocal cord injection if recurrent nerve paresis is identified
Empiric antibiotic therapy and tracheostomy tube placement
Maintenance of NPO until she passes a speech and swallow evaluation

stem: A 50-year-old woman underwent sigmoid colon resection for obstruction by a benign lipoma. During surgery, she became difficult to oxygenate and fecal material was noted in her mouth on suctioning. Now on postoperative day 6 she requires maximal ventilatory support including 100% oxygen and a PEEP of 15 cm H2O. She desaturates to 70% with simple turning. She is on 15 µg/min of levophed and 0.04 units/min of vasopressin to sustain a systolic pressure of 90-100 mmHg. Her urine output for the past 3 hours has been 15 mL, 10 mL, and 5 mL, respectively. Veno-arterial ECMO with cannulation of femoral artery and femoral vein
Veno-venous ECMO with cannulation of internal jugular vein with a bi-caval dual lumen cannula
Veno-venous ECMO with cannulation of internal jugular vein and femoral vein

Other CT findings include a large subdural hematoma causing a midline shift, a Grade I splenic injury, and a right femur fracture. stem: A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue and progressive dyspnea due to severe mitral regurgitation. The left ventricular ejection fraction is 50% and coronary angiography showed no significant coronary artery disease. Robotic mitral valve repair with triangular resection of the posterior leaflet and band annuloplasty reinforced by a pledgeted sutures at both fibrous trigones is completed. After weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass the blood pressure is now 82/56 mmHg despite volume and pressors. Pulmonary artery pressure is 65/42 mmHg, cardiac output is 3.1 L/min, and the ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Intraoperative echocardiography shows a new posterior wall motion abnormality and confirms excellent mitral valve repair with trivial mitral regurgitation. The management is
options: Sternotomy with a vein bypass to the circumflex coronary artery
Inotropic support and placement of intra-aortic balloon pump
Coronary catheterization and stenting of the right coronary artery
ECMO and transport to the intensive care unit for stabilization

stem: A 42-year-old woman is at postoperative day 5 from mechanical aortic valve replacement. Her temporary pacing wires and mediastinal drainage tubes were removed on postoperative day 3. Last night she became acutely unstable and developed complete heart block, for which transcutaneous pacing is initiated. After transfer to the ICU a transvenous pacing pulmonary artery (PA) catheter is placed. Shortly after that she becomes tachypneic and is gasping for air. Her central venous pressure and pulmonary artery pressures show sudden elevations in filling pressures. Auscultation reveals a "splashing" noise. The best next step is
options: Inotropic support with epinephrine and milrinone
Intubation, 100% oxygen, Trendelenburg positioning and left side down
Emergent chest exploration and evacuation of pericardial hematoma
Intubation and transport for CT scan to rule out a saddle embolus

stem: A 61-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and 2+ lower extremity edema. His workup revealed severe mitral stenosis and severe tricuspid regurgitation. Mitral valve replacement and tricuspid valve annuloplasty were done 3 days ago. Heparin was started for persistent rapid atrial fibrillation and an amiodarone bolus dose of 150 mg x 2 was followed by a continuous IV drip. He received a total of 1,350 mg of IV amiodarone over a 24-hour period. The following day he appeared jaundiced and his serum aminotransferase and bilirubin levels were markedly elevated. His alkaline phosphatase level, however, was normal. The best management is
options: Echocardiography to evaluate for failed tricuspid valve repair
Abdominal sonography to rule out acute cholecystitis

stem: A 71 -year-old man presented with acute coronary syndrome. Emergent catheterization and placement of an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) was followed by coronary artery bypass surgery for multivessel disease. Epinephrine and milrinone were required for stabilization. Now, on postoperative day 1, the left ventricular ejection fraction is 25%. Hemodynamics are improving slowly but the milrinone and epinephrine cannot be weaned. His laboratory data show reactive leukocytosis; the platelet count is 66,000/mcL, and his creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies are negative. The best management is
options: Continue current treatment and ICU support
Start aspirin and clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy

stem: A 56-year-old woman is at postoperative day 33 after permanent left ventricular assist device (LVAD) placement. She complains of diffuse abdominal pain and distention without diarrhea. She has been readmitted to ICU with hypotension, left ventricular assist device suction events, and an acute kidney injury. Her WBC count is 49,000/mcL and a C. difficile toxin panel is pending. The patient has received IV antibiotics off and on during her prolonged hospitalization and is on empiric cefepime therapy for hospital-acquired pneumonia. The best next step is to
options: Isolate the patient, continue present antibiotics, and await C. diff toxin result
Start IV vancomycin, add IV metronidazole, and place a rectal tube
Start oral vancomycin, add IV metronidazole, discontinue cefepime, and consult surgery

options: Transfuse the patient to keep hemoglobin at 12 g/dL
Maintain systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg above baseline
Maintain cerebral spinal fluid pressure between 10-15 mmHg

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a mid-distal cT3Nx esophageal carcinoma was initially treated with induction chemoradiation. Restaging studies showed a residual esophageal mass and no new disease. She underwent bronchoscopy and a minimally invasive Ivor Lewis esophagogastrectomy, laparoscopic feeding jejunostomy tube placement, and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Her postoperative course was unremarkable and she was well with the exception of draining 1350 mL of serous fluid from her chest tube on postoperative day 1. Trickle tube feedings at 10 mL per hour were started on postoperative day 2 and the chest tube drainage increased to 2060 mL that day. The thoracostomy tube output was 2730 mL on postoperative 3 and it developed a milky appearance. Triglycerides in the fluid were 314 mg/dL. The current CXR is shown. The best next step is
options: Chemical pleurodesis via the indwelling chest tube
Right thoracotomy and mass ligation of the thoracic duct
Barium swallow to evaluate for anastomotic leak
Upper endoscopy and esophageal stent placement

Selected images from a contrast esophagram performed on postoperative day 6 are shown. The patient's WBC count is 8,700/mcL. A 68-year-old woman was previously treated with oral antibiotics for C. difficile infection. She was diagnosed with carcinoid tumor of the right colon with resectable metastatic disease to the right lobe of the liver. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild-to-moderate right ventricular (RV) dysfunction with severe tricuspid and pulmonary regurgitation. Despite aggressive diuretic therapy, she continued to have bilateral lower extremity edema and ascites. She was taken to the operating room where an intra-aortic balloon was placed initially. Tricuspid and pulmonary valves were replaced along with bovine pericardial patch enlargement of her pulmonary artery. Post-cardiopulmonary bypass echocardiography clips are shown. Her oxygen saturation is 100% on PEEP at 5 cm H2O and 100% O2. Her left ventricular function is mildly depressed. The best next step is
options: Place a percutaneous right-sided ImpellaTM device
Place a saphenous vein graft to the right coronary artery

He is currently intubated and sedated. He is now afebrile with heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 124/84 mmHg, and SpO2 90%. Arterial blood gas values are: pH 7.32, pCO2 52 torr, pO2 63 torr. Change to airway pressure release ventilation

His hospital course was complicated by recurrent episodes of atrial fibrillation and a deep venous thrombosis. He reports that he was doing well until a few days ago when he began to notice increasing shortness of breath. His current medications include amiodarone 400 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, aspirin 81 mg daily, rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a recent urinary tract infection.
